senses.gloss:
Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa
------------------------------------------
Among the luminaries of the भक्ति Movement that energized the Hindu masses during the middle ages, the greatest, perhaps, was श्रीकृष्ण चैतन्य (A.D. 1485-1533), more commonly known as चैतन्य महाप्रभु. His teachings gradually got metamorphosed into a system of philosophy, now well-known as the Acintyabhedābheda school. बलदेव विद्याभूषण who lived in the early 18th century, is an important writer of this school. He was born in a village near Remuna in Orissa. He was a pupil of Vairāgi Pītāmbara Dāsa. Out of the 14 works attributed to him, the Govinda-bhāṣya, a commentary on the Brahma-sūtras is most well-known. It has a subcommentary called Sūkṣma, the author of which is unknown.

Balipratipadā
------------------------------------------
Considered as one of the three most holy days of the Hindu चलेन्दर्, बलि-prati-padā falls on the Kārttika śukla-pratipad (first day of the bright fortnight of the month Kārttika, generally in November). It is also one of the three days of the दीपावली (also spelt as दिवाली) festival, the festival of lights. It was on this day, according to the Hindu म्य्थोलोग्य्, that बलि, the emperor of the असुरस् or demons, was conquered by Lord विष्णु and was granted several boons since he was a great devotee.
Worship of an image of बलि along with that of his consort Vindhyāvalī, is an important item of the festival, especially for kings. Gifts given on this day produce manifold results.
Worship of cows and bulls as also the hill गोवर्धन (See ANNAKŪṬA.), tying of the Mārgapālī (lit., protectress of the road) or a rope of कुश grass between a pole and a tree across a road and passing under it, and playing dice, are some of the items generally observed during this festival. A paurāṇic story of the game of dice between शिव and पार्वती seems to be at the back of this practice of dice-play. Hence the name ‘Dyūtapratipadā’ also for this day.
Sometimes, a ceremonial tug-of-war is also arranged in front of a temple or the palace, between the princely class and the commoners, the latter always ‘winning’ at the end! Occasionally, images of अग्नि and ब्रह्मा are established on a रथ or chariot and worshipped. The chariot is then drawn round the streets of the town. Hence this festival is also called ‘Balipratipadā-rathayātrāvrata’.
See also DĪPĀVALĪ.

bālakṛcchra
(‘the small penance’)
------------------------------------------
Pātaka (sin) and प्रायश्चित्त (expi-ation of sin) are two of the widely discussed topics in the smṛtis and धर्मशास्त्रस्. Sins may be serious (mahāpātakas) or minor (upapātakas). The prāyaścittas prescribed for the महापातकस् like killing a ब्राह्मण or incest, often end in the death of the sinner. But, those prescribed for the upapātakas like minor thefts or abandoning the Vedic fires, are tolerable and purify the sinners.
Kṛcchra is a very general name given to most of these prāyaścittas. Bālakṛcchra—also called śiśukṛcchra or laghukṛcchra—is one variety prescribed for upapātakas in which the expiation is light and easy. If kṛcchras are usually spread over 12 days, बालकृच्छ्र is observed only for 4 days. It consists in eating once only in day time on the first day, once only in the night on the second day, eating ड़ोओद् that comes unasked, that too only once, on the third day and, ड़स्तिन्ग् on the fourth day. Other general rules as applicable to kṛcchras like bathing thrice daily, speaking the truth and so on, should also be followed.
See KṚCCHRA and CĀNDRĀYAṆA.

bala
(‘strength;’ ‘armed forces’)
------------------------------------------
The literal meaning of the word ‘bala’ is ‘strength.’ However, the word is often used in a metaphorical sense, as for instance in statements like ‘dhigbalaṁ kṣattriyabalaṁ brahmatejobalaṁ balam;’ (‘Fie be unto the power of the क्षत्त्रिय! The power of lustre of ब्रह्मन् is verily the power!’). There are other interesting statements such as: vāṇijya (trade) is the बल of a वैश्य; युद्ध (war) is the बल of a क्षत्त्रिय; dhana (wealth) is the बल of a rich man; rodana (crying) is the बल of a child; अनृत (falsehood) is the बल of thieves; परमात्मन् (God) is the बल of devotees and so on.
Works on Hindu political science like the Arthaśāstra of कौटिल्य (300 B.C.) declare that a rājya or state is constituted by seven elements like svāmin (ruler or sovereign), अमात्य (minister), जनपद or rāṣṭra (the territory of the State and its people) and so on. दण्ड or बल (armed forces) is one of these seven constituents.
Most of the ancient and early medieval works state that a big army should consist of four constituents; hence the name ‘caturaṅga-बल,’ ‘armed forces with four parts’. They are hasti (elephants), aśva (horses), रथ (chariots) and padāti (foot-soldiers).
The works also mention six kinds of troops: maula (hereditary troops), bhṛta or bhṛtaka (mercenary troops), śreṇi (guild troops), मित्र (troops of an ally), amitra (troops that once belonged to an enemy) and aṭavī or āṭavika (wild tribes as troops). The earlier varieties of troops are superior to the later ones.
The Mahābhārata declares that out of the several balas of a king like bāhubala (brute force), dhanabala (power of wealth), amātyabala (power due to the right type of ministers) and so on, prajñābala (power of wisdom) is the greatest (Udyogaparva 37.52-55).
Balarāma, कृष्ण’s elder brother is also known as बल. (For details see BALARĀMA.)

Bālāki
(‘Son of Balākā’)
------------------------------------------
The Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (2.1) mentions one sage बालाकि (Son of the lady Balākā) who was गार्ग्य (a descendant of the sage गर्ग). He was nicknamed ‘Dṛpta-बालाकि’ since he was a vain person (dṛpta = vain). He had mastered one aspect of the knowledge of ब्रह्मन्. He went to the king अजातशत्रु of काशी and expressed his desire to teach him. The king, who was more learned, and could see through his vanity, proved his superi-ority. Then बालाकि became his disciple and learnt about the ब्रह्मन् without attributes.
Bālāki is also one of the names of the hundred sons of the king Dhṛtarāṣtṛa, the ड़थेर् of दुर्योधन.

Bali
(‘that which is brought’)
------------------------------------------
Like प्रह्लाद, बलि is another great name among the असुरस् or demons who were devotees of Lord विष्णु. Actually, he was the grandson of the former and the son of विरोचन. After losing his life in a battle with इन्द्र, the king of देवस् or gods, he was revived by his गुरु शुक्राचार्य. He then performed severe austerities, got some divine weapons and then usurped स्वर्ग, the Kingdom of इन्द्र, after worsting him in the battle. When the gods appealed to Lord विष्णु to restore their domain back to them, विष्णु incarnated himself as वामन, the Dwarf, approached बलि, who was well-known as extraordinarily generous, for a gift of land and occupied all the three worlds in the process of receiving it. He also pushed बलि down into the nether world and restored to इन्द्र and the gods, their lost स्वर्ग. बलि became the इन्द्र later, in another cycle of च्रेअतिओन्, known as Sāvarṇika मन्वन्तर. He is listed among the eight चिरजीविन्स् (those who are immortal).
See also PRAHLĀDA and VĀMANA.

Bālājī
------------------------------------------
See TIRUPATI and VEṄKAṬEŚVARA.

Bālasubrahmaṇya
(‘the boy सुब्रह्मण्य’)
------------------------------------------
Subrahmaṇya—also known by several other names such as कुमार, स्कन्द, कार्त्तिकेय, षण्मुख and Guha—is a very popular Hindu deity in South India, especially in Tamil Nadu. He is the son of शिव and पार्वती and the elder brother of गणेश. Many heroic exploits are attributed to him including the leading of the armies of the gods and killing the formidable demon तारकासुर. Most of these were accomplished when he was still a ‘bāla’ or boy. Hence he is more often represented as ‘Bāla-सुब्रह्मण्य’. Iconographical works describe him as red in colour, with only two hands, holding a lotus in the right and keeping the left on the waist.
See also SUBRAHMAṆYA.

Balapramathinī
(‘destroyer of strength’)
------------------------------------------
Śakti or divine power of God is often pictured as a goddess, as the consort of the Deity. For instance, पार्वती is the power of शिव, personified as his consort. Out of the several such goddesses, all being the aspects of the supreme शक्ति, बलप्रमथिनी is a minor one. Since सूर्य or Sun is hot and enervating, this deity represents the Sun as a tattva or principle. She is pictured as white or reddish in complexion and has two hands carrying a कपाल (skull) and a पाश (noose). She is the destroyer of all enemies and hence propitiated as such. Her consort is Ugra, a terrible aspect of शिव.

Balarāma
(‘Rāma of strength’)
------------------------------------------
Balarāma was the elder brother of कृष्ण. He was conceived as the seventh son of देवकी by Vasudeva. But the foetus was drawn out of her by योगमाया (divine power) and placed in the womb of रोहिणी, the elder wife of Vasudeva, living at Nandagokula. So he was born as the son of रोहिणी. Since he was extraordinarily strong, he was called ‘Balarāma’ (bala = strength). He had several other names like सङ्कर्षण, Rauhiṇeya, Musalī, Halī, Nīlāmbara and so on. As per the paurāṇic lore, he was the इन्चर्नतिओन् of आदिशेष (the serpent on which विष्णु is resting in the Kṣīrasāgara or ocean of milk) come down to help कृष्ण who was विष्णु himself. He was an expert in fighting with गदा or mace. The plough (halā) was his favourite weapon. The Bhāgavata is full of his exploits. Along with कृष्ण, he too killed many a demon like Pralamba, Dhenuka, Dvivida and Balvala. After the killing of कṁस by कृष्ण, बलराम too got his formal एदुचतिओन् under the sage सान्दीपनि. He married Revatī, the daughter of the king Revata. When the Kauravas of हस्तिनापुर had abducted Sāmba, a son of कृष्ण, he went there and rescued him. It was he who taught गदा-विद्या (the science of fighting with the mace) to भीम (the second of the five Pāṇḍavas) and दुर्योधन (the eldest of the Kauravas). He had a soft corner for the latter.
During the कुरुक्षेत्र (or Mahā-bhārata) war, he refused to participate but went away on a पिल्ग्रिमगे. He reappeared at the time of the duel between भीम and दुर्योधन. He tried to prevent it but did not succeed. He was cross with भीम for having flouted the rules of mace-fighting but was pacified by कृष्ण.
When the Yādavas exterminated one another in mutual fighting, बलराम sat in योग and left the body in the form of a serpent thus confirming that he was आदिशेष.
See also KṚṢṆA.

Baladeva
------------------------------------------
In the Hindu mythological lore ‘Baladeva’ is one of the several names by which बलराम, the elder brother of कृष्ण, was known.

Bālakrīḍā
------------------------------------------
Smṛtis are secondary scriptures which expound धर्म, in consonance with the Śruti or the वेदस्. If the Śruti gives the general spiritual truths, the smṛtis give elaborate details pertaining to the code of conduct of an individual member of the society both at the personal and at the social level. One of the earliest smṛtis that ranks on almost equal terms with the Manusmṛti, is the Yājñavalkya स्मृति. This work has two well-known commentaries: the Mitākṣarā of Vijñā-neśvara (12th cent. A.D.) and the Bālakrīḍā of विश्वरूप (9th cent. A. D.).
Being earlier than the Mitākṣarā, the Bālakrīḍā is a pioneering work. Its author, विश्वरूप shows a good grasp of the पूर्वमीमाṁसा terms and लोगिच्, but seems to lean towards the advaita of शङ्कर (A. D. 788-820) where philosophical ideas are concerned.
Some scholars opine that विश्वरूप and सुरेश्वर, a disciple of शङ्कर, are identical, ‘Viśvarūpa’ being his premonastic name.
See also VIŚVARŪPA and YĀJÑAVALKYA SMṚTI.

balipīṭha
(‘pedestal for offering’)
------------------------------------------
Balipīṭha or a pedestal where balis or ड़ोओद् offerings are made, is an essential part of a Hindu temple. Situated usually near the ध्वजस्तम्भ or the flagpost, but nearer the shrine, it is a raised platform made of stone, the height being generally one-eighth that of the garbha-gṛha or the sanctum sactorum. Materials other than stone, like metal, mud or bricks, may also be used.
The बलिपीठ may be square, rectangular, octagonal, sixteen-sided or circular; and will have several tiers, each tier providing space for a particular class of celestial beings like the dikpālas (guardian deities of the quarters), अप्सरास् (celestial nymphs), piśācas (goblins) and so on, to receive the ड़ोओद् offered.
After the main deity is served with naivedya or ड़ोओद्, the priests begin a procession for feeding the guardian deities and minor deities. The first one to receive the offering is the ‘balibera’ or the movable metallic image, which is then carried in the procession. After circumambulating the main deity, the ड़ोओद् offering is kept on the बलिपीठ.
Balis or ड़ोओद्-offerings are given only in the temple worship and not in the worship at home.

bālālaya
(‘the little temple’)
------------------------------------------
Hindu temples, with their images, are built with materials like stone, so that they can last long. Due to the ravages of time, weather, accidents or any other cause, when the temple structure or the image is damaged, needing repair or replacement, provision has been made in the आगमस् for the necessary ritualistic processes to transfer the ‘kalā’ or the power of the deity temporarily through a कलश (consecrated pitcher of water) to a new image and installed in a new temple provisionally built for the purpose. Once the renovation work is over, the ‘kalā’ is transferred back to the old renovated temple and image.
The temporary structure put up for this purpose to होउसे the deity during the renovation work, so that the usual rituals can go on undisturbed, is technically called ‘bālālaya’ or ‘the little temple’, since it is ‘small’ compared to the original structure. It is generally built in the front of the old temple, but to its left side, and its door facing that of the old one. It should have both a गर्भगृह (sanctum sanctorum) and a मण्डप (hall) attached to it. The image may be made of either metal or wood. The entire process of consecration of the बालालय is identical with that of any newly built temple. Once the old temple is renovated, the कला is transferred back to the old image in the renovated shrine or to the new image installed there, if the old one had been damaged necessitating replacement. After this, the image of the बालालय has to be burnt, if of wood, or melted, if of metal, and presented to the आचार्य or preceptor. The old image of the original temple, if replaced, should be taken in a procession and immersed deeply in sea or river or lake.

Bāla-Gaṇapati
(‘Gaṇapati, the boy’)
------------------------------------------
Among the several gods of the Hindu pantheon, गणपति, the elephant-headed god is one of the most widely worshipped. Temples to him are also legion.
There are several aspects of गणपति, of which बाल-गणपति is one. He is represented iconographically as a boy, holding a mango, a plantain, a jack-fruit and a sugar-cane in his four hands. With his trunk he holds a wood-apple. His colour is that of the rising sun.
See also GAṆAPATI.

Balabhadra
------------------------------------------
This is one of the several names by which बलराम, the elder brother of कृष्ण, was known. See BALARĀMA for details.

baliharaṇa
(‘distributing the balis or offerings’)
------------------------------------------
‘Baliharaṇa’ is the same as ‘bhūta-यज्ञ’, one of the पञ्चयज्ञस् or five daily sacrifices to be performed by every householder. The balis or offerings of cooked rice are kept on the ground, properly cleaned, to be accepted by the domestic deities, by the deities of water, of herbs and others. As part of this rite, ड़ोओद् is to be offered to other human beings in need of the same, as also animals, out of compassion.
See also VAIŚVADEVA.

Bālakāṇḍa
------------------------------------------
This is the first book of the well-known epic Rāmāyaṇa of वाल्मीकि.
See RĀMĀYAṆA for details.

Balavikaraṇī
(‘that which augments strength’)
------------------------------------------
She is one of the several aspects of the मोथेर् Goddess whose worship will endow the votary with strength and peace. She is also classed, sometimes, among the परिवारदेवतास् or attendant deities of the Divine मोथेर्. Iconographically, she is described as grey in colour with long eyes and two hands holding a कपाल (skull) and अक्षमाला (rosary).
Occasionally she is stated to be the personification of the principle of the मोओन् (candratattva), responsible for the vigorous growth of oṣadhis or medical herbs. In this aspect, she is considered to be the consort of महादेव (Śiva).
See also SUBRAHMAṆYA.

balasiddhi
(‘power of physical strength’)
------------------------------------------
The Yogasūtras of पतञ्जलि (200 B.C.) is accepted as a basic text of योग and has been highly venerated. In the third chapter of the work called Vibhūtipāda, various vibhūtis or सिद्धिस् (supernatural powers) that a योगि obtains by the practice of ‘saṁyama’ are described; and बलसिद्धि is one of them. सṁयम is a technical term used to indicate the triad of धारणा (fixing the मिन्द् on the object of concentration), ध्यान (meditation) and समाधि (total absorption in the object thus chosen), practised on one and the same object. This सṁयम results in the development or manifestation of supernatural powers in the योगि.
If सṁयम is practised on the strength of an elephant (vide Yogasūtras 3.24) or lion or the mythical bird गरुड or हनुमान् (the devotee of राम), the योगि develops a strength similar to theirs. This is called ‘balasiddhi’.
